z-m-08-04.title: High jump records: who jump higher?
z-m-08-04.topic: Compare one-decimal-place number with three-decimal-place number
z-m-08-04.goal: Compare decimals by place value, no be by how many digits dem get; check your judgment as new data come, and make your own counterexample to wrong rule.
z-m-08-04.material: For school sports day high jump, dem measure Seoyun and Dohyeon records. Record na height in meters (m) from floor to bar, measured with tape. Dem go give you the records one step at a time.
z-m-08-04.thinking.0: Check your judgment as data dey add
z-m-08-04.thinking.1: Compare decimal sizes by place value
z-m-08-04.prereq.0: Read and write decimals with one, two and three decimal places
z-m-08-04.s.s1.prompt: Look data one piece at a time, judge who jump higher, then check your judgment wen new data arrive.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, judge using only wetin you know so far, and first write with words whether your judgment change wen new data come.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.hint.1: Change the two records to the same unit and compare them side by side.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Seoyun record na 1.4 m and Dohyeon record na 1.38 m.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you only look digits, wetin you think now?
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.after: For this step, both judgment say Seoyun higher and judgment say e too early to decide make sense. You fit decide by first comparing tenths places.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Maybe na judgment wey look place values for tenths and hundredths places.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Dohyeon jump higher, because 38 bigger than 4
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read digits after decimal point like whole number, then compare 38 and 4. With decimals, you must first look which place each digit dey.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: E hard to decide from the digits alone
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: E reasonable to admit say you no sure and wait for next data too.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Tape get big marks wey divide the part above 1 m into 10 spaces, and if you divide each space again into 10, total na 100 spaces. Seoyun 1.4 m na 4 spaces above 1 m on big marks. Dohyeon 1.38 m na 38 spaces above 1 m on the 100-space marks.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now wey you don see the scale data, who you think higher?
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.after: 1.4 m na same as 1.40 m, so na 40 sections. Even with fewer digits, number fit bigger because of place value.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: On the 100-section scale, 1.4 na 40 sections, so e pass 38 sections.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Check again on scale say number 38 less than 40.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Both records dey on the scale, so you fit decide with this data.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Harin jump too. Harin record na 1.405 m. And Seoyun 1.4 m na same height whether you write 1.40 m or 1.400 m.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which one list the three records from highest to lowest?
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.after: 1.405 na 0.005 higher than 1.400. So order na Harin, Seoyun, Dohyeon. Order of Seoyun and Dohyeon no change wen new data come.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Na order wey you get if you think say the one with more digits bigger. Write 1.4 as 1.400 and compare starting from tenths place.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 1.405 and 1.4 (= 1.400) first differ for thousandths place, and 1.38 differ for hundredths place.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Seoyun and Harin same, and Dohyeon lowest
z-m-08-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You ignore the 5 at end of 1.405. 1.400 and 1.405 different numbers.
z-m-08-04.s.s1.reflect: Even when new data come, judgment say Seoyun jump higher than Dohyeon remain the same. Wetin change na the order after Harin join. Compare decimals by place value for each digit, no be by how many digits dey.
z-m-08-04.s.s2.prompt: One friend talk, 'Number wey get more digits after decimal point na the bigger number.' Use two new decimals apart from 1.4, 1.38 and 1.405 wey you see above, show say this statement wrong and write which one bigger.
z-m-08-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think of two decimals wey tenths digits different.
z-m-08-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write bigger number to hundredths place (add zero) and compare side by side. The added digit is 0. 0
z-m-08-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In decimals you give, is one with more digits always smaller?
z-m-08-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You remember same value fit use different number of decimal digits (1.4=1.40)? 1.4 1.40
z-m-08-04.s.s2.model.0: Look 0.5 and 0.45. 0.45 get more digits, but 0.5=0.50, bigger than 0.45. 0.5 0.45 0.45 0.5 0.50 0.45
z-m-08-04.s.s2.model.2: 0.9 and 0.89: 0.89 get two decimal digits, but 0.9=0.90, so 0.9 bigger. 0.9 0.89 0.89 0.9 0.90 0.9

z-m-08-07.title: How many digits does number made by two cards have?
z-m-08-07.topic: Estimating product size and digit count
z-m-08-07.goal: Test general claim with counterexamples; estimate smallest/largest cases, state possible result range and conditions.
z-m-08-07.material: Make products using cards: choose 3-digit number (100-999) and 2-digit (10-99), multiply. Minseo says, '3-digit times 2-digit always 5 digits, because 3+2=5!' 100 999 10 99 3 2 5
z-m-08-07.thinking.0: Choosing examples likely to be counterexamples
z-m-08-07.thinking.2: Estimating range and concluding with conditions
z-m-08-07.prereq.0: Multiplying 3-digit by 2-digit by estimate or calculation (Grade 4) 4
z-m-08-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all card pairs that show Minseo wrong. Estimate before calculating.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each pair, round numbers to nearest hundred/ten and estimate product.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.hint.1: Sort choices whether product below or above 10000. 10000
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.a: Estimate product of biggest numbers; how many digits?
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.c: Is 500×40 in thousands or ten-thousands? Can this pair challenge claim? 500 40
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.d: This is product of two smallest cards.
z-m-08-07.s.s1.r.e: Estimate whether 120×50 in thousands or ten-thousands. 120 50
z-m-08-07.s.s1.explain: To challenge claim need pair giving four-digit product. 345×27=9315, 100×10=1000, 120×50=6000 all four digits. 999×99=98901 and 500×40=20000 five digits, so no counterexample. 345 27 9315 100 10 1000 120 50 6000 999 99 98901 500 40 20000
z-m-08-07.s.s2.prompt: Test Minseo claim. Choose 3-digit a and 2-digit b for one 4-digit product and one 5-digit product. (Digit counts must differ.)
z-m-08-07.s.s2.hint.0: Start with small values, count digits for product like 100×10. 100 10
z-m-08-07.s.s2.hint.1: Estimate which a or b need increase and by how much for product pass 10000. 10000
z-m-08-07.s.s3.prompt: What can you say about digit count for 3-digit ×2-digit? Explain by estimating/calculating smallest and biggest.
z-m-08-07.s.s3.hint.1: Estimate product of biggest two numbers compared with 100×100. 100 100
z-m-08-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Find digit count for smallest 100×10 and largest 999×99? 100 10 999 99
z-m-08-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You explain how every in-between product has 4 or 5 digits?
z-m-08-07.s.s3.model.0: Product gets 4 or 5 digits. Smallest 100×10=1000 has 4; largest 999×99 <100000, so not 6 digits. Between them, it becomes 5 digits after exceeding 10000. 100 10 1000 999 99 100000 10000
z-m-08-07.s.s3.model.1: Product fit get 4 or 5 digits. 345×27=9315 has 4, 500×40=20000 has 5. It can't be below 1000 or above 100000. 4 5 345 27 9315 500 40 20000 1000
z-m-08-07.s.s3.model.2: Product has 4 or 5 digits. Smallest 100×10=1000 is 4 digits; largest 999×99 is less than 100000, at most 5 digits. 100 10 1000 999 99

z-m-08-02.title: Two cards wey total 90: their scores go be the same too?
z-m-08-02.topic: Compare products of two two-digit numbers
z-m-08-02.goal: Understand say one example no fit confirm 'always the same'; make different examples wey meet condition, compare them, then describe wetin pairs with bigger scores get in common.
z-m-08-02.material: Make we play number card game. Each card get one natural number from 10 to 99. Rule: choose two cards and the two numbers must total exactly 90. Score na the two numbers multiplied together. Sua choose 40 and 50 and get 2000 points. Then she talk, 'If total na 90, score always na 2000 points!' The order wey you put cards no matter. (30 and 60, and 60 and 30, na the same pair.)
z-m-08-02.thinking.0: Tell apart wetin one example show and wetin e no show
z-m-08-02.thinking.2: Compare examples and guess the rule
z-m-08-02.prereq.0: Multiply two-digit numbers together (Grade 4 level, no calculator)
z-m-08-02.prereq.1: Pair natural numbers so total go be the same
z-m-08-02.s.s1.prompt: Sua talk after she see the result for one pair 40 and 50. Wetin this one pair result tell us about wetin Sua talk?
z-m-08-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sua statement get the word 'always'. Think the quickest thing to do to find out whether statement true.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.hint.1: Make one more pair with total 90 and find the score.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.a: 40 and 50 give 2000 points, so any pair give 2000 points
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.a: One example being correct no prove 'always'. How about test other pairs too?
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.b: We no fit decide until we check another pair with total 90
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.b: You point out say one example alone no fit tell us 'always'.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.c: We fit decide right now say scores no be the same even if totals same
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.c: Result of only one pair no fit confirm 'not the same'. You need actually make other pairs and compare them.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.o.d: We no know yet. So we no need check any other pair
z-m-08-02.s.s1.r.d: Correct to feel say you no know, but wen you no know, testing na the next step.
z-m-08-02.s.s1.explain: 40 and 50 giving 2000 points na just one example wey no contradict Sua statement. To know whether 'if total na 90, score always the same' true, you must check other pairs wey total 90. If another pair give different score, that pair na counterexample.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 pairs of two-digit cards wey total 90 and their scores different. (If you swap the cards, na the same pair.)
z-m-08-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the first card, then subtract that number from 90 to make second card.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.hint.1: Change the first card, from 10 up to 90, but check say both numbers get two digits.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Cards get only natural numbers written on them.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The numbers on cards na two-digit numbers from 10 to 99.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The two numbers no total 90. Add them to check.
z-m-08-02.s.s2.explain: Pairs wey total 90 get different scores, like (40, 50) = 2000 points, (30, 60) = 1800 points, (20, 70) = 1400 points, (45, 45) = 2025 points, and (11, 79) = 869 points. Since some pairs get same total but different products, Sua statement no always correct. Swapped pair (50 and 40) na same pair, so count am once only.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.prompt: Compare the scores for the pairs wey you make. How the two numbers look for the pair with biggest score? Describe one way to choose cards so score go bigger. Use pairs wey you really find as examples.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write scores of pairs you make from biggest to smallest, and also write difference between the two numbers for each pair.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how far apart the two numbers be in pairs with big scores and pairs with small scores.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Pair with biggest score na ...
z-m-08-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You really multiply to find scores for your examples?
z-m-08-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You fit test one more time whether a new pair wey you choose with the method you describe really get bigger score?
z-m-08-02.s.s3.model.0: 40 and 50 give 2000 points, 30 and 60 give 1800 points, and 20 and 70 give 1400 points. The nearer the two numbers be, the bigger the score. So if I choose numbers with small difference like 45 and 45, I think e go bigger again.
z-m-08-02.s.s3.model.1: The smaller the difference between the pair, the bigger the score. Difference between 40 and 50 na 10 and score na 2000, but 20 and 70 get difference 50 and give 1400. If total na 90, e good to choose numbers near 45.

z-m-08-06.title: If you join two ribbons, go total be 4m? 4
z-m-08-06.goal: Judge if given info enough for conclusion, state missing info, and express with numbers how conclusion change by condition.
z-m-08-06.material: To tie around box once need at least 4m string. Two ribbons: red 2.4m, blue 1.65m. Want join as one. Not yet decided end-to-end tape or overlap/glue. 4 2.4 1.65
z-m-08-06.thinking.2: Writing numeric conclusions that depend on conditions
z-m-08-06.s.s1.prompt: With current info, can we say ribbon tie box?
z-m-08-06.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine both joining methods and write total length for each.
z-m-08-06.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, state assumption about joining needed for claim true.
z-m-08-06.s.s1.o.a: Can't tell. Need know which ribbon wound first
z-m-08-06.s.s1.r.a: Winding order no effect on total length. Find info affecting length.
z-m-08-06.s.s1.o.b: Can't tell; depend how they join, need more info
z-m-08-06.s.s1.r.b: You notice overlap length depend on joining method.
z-m-08-06.s.s1.r.c: Adding ribbon lengths okay so far. But does total stay same depending on joining?
z-m-08-06.s.s1.o.d: Can't tie. 1.65 shorter than 2.4, so not 4 1.65 2.4 4
z-m-08-06.s.s1.r.d: Joining uses full lengths of both. Recheck why judged only by shorter ribbon.
z-m-08-06.s.s1.explain: End-to-end join keeps 4.05m, enough. Overlap makes shorter; need overlap length to decide. Method not decided, so 'need more info' right. Only assuming end-to-end can we say enough. 4.05
z-m-08-06.s.s2.prompt: You choose overlap/glue. Overlap x can be whole cm from 1 to 8. Give 3 different x values where joined ribbon still at least 4m. 1 8 4

z-m-08-06.s.s2.hint.1: Change overlap by 1cm each time and check joined length at least 400cm. 1 400
z-m-08-06.s.s2.ok.c1: Overlap length whole number of cm.
z-m-08-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Overlap must be at least 1cm and at most 8cm. 1 8
z-m-08-06.s.s2.fail.c3: Joined length below 4m (400cm). Convert ribbons to cm, add, subtract overlap to check. 4 400
z-m-08-06.s.s2.explain: Red 2.4m=240cm, blue 1.65m=165cm, total 405cm. After subtracting overlap, to stay at least 400cm overlap must be 5cm or less. 1,2,3,4,5cm work; from 6cm it falls short. No-overlap 0cm also enough, but task assumes overlap/glue. The steps use 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 400cm. 2.4 240 1.65 165 405 400 5 1 2 3 4 5 6 400 0
z-m-08-06.s.s3.prompt: If overlap and glue, how decide if ribbon tie box? Explain using 4.05m and overlap length. 4.05
z-m-08-06.s.s3.hint.0: Convert difference between 4.05m and 4m to cm. 4.05 4
z-m-08-06.s.s3.hint.1: Say what happen if overlap less or more than this difference.

z-m-08-06.s.s3.model.0: When overlap-joining, subtract overlap from 4.05m. 4.05 is 0.05m (5cm) more than 4, so overlap 5cm or less leaves 4m enough; over 5cm no. 4.05 4.05 0.05 5 4 5 4 5
z-m-08-06.s.s3.model.1: No overlap gives 4.05m, enough, but overlap changes it. 4.05−4=0.05m, so over 5cm falls short. 4.05 4.05 4 0.05 5

z-m-08-01.title: Minjae calculation table for page count in 23 books
z-m-08-01.topic: Place value when multiply 3-digit by 2-digit number
z-m-08-01.goal: Find line where place value error happened in column multiplication; check by estimate and last digit, rewrite correctly.
z-m-08-01.material: Library buy 23 storybooks, each 346 pages. Minjae use column multiplication to find total. No picture, so table described in words, line by line.
z-m-08-01.thinking.1: Checking result by estimate and last digit
z-m-08-01.prereq.0: Reading column multiplication and ones/tens/hundreds values (Grade 4)
z-m-08-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose first wrong line in Minjae table.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, say what value multiplier has (which place digit 2 belong to).
z-m-08-01.s.s1.hint.1: Estimate pages for 20 books ×346, compare with 1730.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.line.0: Write 23 under 346 and start with 3 in ones place.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.line.2: Multiply by 2 in tens place too. Write 346×2=692, with right end directly under 1038.
z-m-08-01.s.s1.explain: First error line 3. 2 in 23 is tens digit, means 20, not 2. So 346×2=692 must shift one place left (read as 6920). Line 4 addition 1038+692=1730 correct alone, but addends wrong; line 5 follows that. The wrong line writes 346×2=692.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all reasons you can tell 1730 pages wrong without finishing calculation.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.hint.0: First estimate roughly how many times one-book page count the 23 books should have.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.hint.1: Without calculating, mark each choice true/false, then check if true ones conflict with 1730.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.b: 346 and 23 both even, so product even, but 1730 odd
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.b: 23 odd and 1730 even. Before even/odd reasoning, check exactly which numbers multiplied.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.c: 6×3=18, so product ones digit must be 8, but 1730 ends in 0
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.c: Checking last digit by multiplying ones digits is useful too.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.d: Since 692 smaller than 1038, total 1730 must be smaller than 1038
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.d: Adding two numbers make result bigger than either one. Look again how to compare total with one of the numbers.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.o.e: Each book get 346 pages and 23 books dey, so answer must pass 346, and 1730 pass 346
z-m-08-01.s.s2.r.e: True say 1730 pass 346. But that alone no show say 1730 wrong. You need estimate a more fitting size.
z-m-08-01.s.s2.explain: If you estimate 300 × 20 = 6000, answer must pass 6000 pages, and from multiplying ones digits, 6 × 3 = 18, last digit must be 8. Neither reason fit 1730. Even/odd reason (b) wrong because 23 odd, and d and e no be evidence say 1730 wrong.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Minjae calculation table and find correct number of pages. Also use your own words explain why the line wey you change must change that way.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write what value the 2 for tens place mean.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write results of 346 × 2 and 346 × 20 side by side, then compare which one belong for correct line.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The 2 for tens place na ...
z-m-08-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You write why number wey multiply with 346 in corrected calculation na 20 (or value like 6920) instead of 2?
z-m-08-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You check by estimating or using last digit say your method (add 0, shift one place left, multiply by 20) match 7958 pages?
z-m-08-01.s.s3.model.0: 346 × 20 = 6920. The 2 for tens place na 20, so you must write 6920, no be 692. 1038 + 6920 = 7958 pages.
z-m-08-01.s.s3.model.1: Shift 692 one place to the left. Wen you multiply by digit for tens place, ones place empty, so you must think say 0 dey there. 1038 + 6920 = 7958, so e na 7958 pages.

z-m-08-03.title: Pack 14 into each box so the leftover pieces be odd number
z-m-08-03.topic: Connection between quotient and remainder in division
z-m-08-03.goal: Learn the range wey leftover fit be, make different examples of dividend, quotient and leftover wey meet conditions, then explain why the range be like that.
z-m-08-03.material: Chocolate factory pack exactly 14 chocolates in each box. Dem count full boxes only, and dem leave aside the loose pieces wey no fill a box. Call number of chocolates made a, number of full boxes q and loose pieces left aside r. (a dey between 100 and 999.)
z-m-08-03.thinking.0: Tell possible cases apart from impossible cases
z-m-08-03.thinking.1: Make examples wey meet plenty conditions at once
z-m-08-03.prereq.1: Know the relationship divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend
z-m-08-03.s.s1.prompt: Chocolates go into boxes of 14, and at least 1 loose piece remain. Choose all the numbers wey loose pieces r fit be.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think wetin fit happen to the leftover if 14 pieces remain.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, check one by one whether leftover pieces fit fill one more box.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.a: If 14 pieces remain, you fit put those 14 inside one box. Wetin go happen to number of boxes then?
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.b: You think of case where less than 14 pieces remain.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.c: If 17 pieces remain, you fit fill one more box. How many remain after that? Think again the most wey fit remain.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.d: Na case where only one piece miss to fill a box.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.e: If 28 pieces remain, you fit fill two more boxes. Think again the range for leftover.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.r.f: You find case where less than 14 remain.
z-m-08-03.s.s1.explain: Dem count full boxes only, so if 14 or more loose pieces remain, you fit fill more boxes. So leftover fit only be from 1 to 13. 5, 13 and 9 possible; 14, 17 and 28 no possible.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different cases where chocolate number a, full boxes q and loose pieces r all meet these conditions. Conditions: number of boxes na 10 or more and 99 or less, and loose pieces na odd number.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.hint.0: First choose number of boxes q, then find how many chocolates fit inside q boxes of 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.hint.1: Add odd number of loose pieces to that to make a, then check say loose pieces less than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c1: All three numbers na natural numbers.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The counts must be natural numbers.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Number of chocolates dey between 100 and 999.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Number of chocolates made must dey between 100 and 999.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c3: Number of boxes na 10 or more and 99 or less.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Number of full boxes must be 10 or more and 99 or less.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c4: Chocolates packed in boxes plus loose pieces equal number of chocolates made.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c4: Add chocolates inside boxes of 14 and loose pieces, then check whether total equal a.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c5: Number of loose pieces less than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c5: If 14 or more loose pieces remain, you fit fill more boxes. Loose pieces left must be less than 14.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.ok.c6: Number of loose pieces na odd.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.fail.c6: Number of loose pieces no be odd.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 14 × 12 + 5 = 173, so 173 chocolates fill 12 boxes and 5 loose pieces remain. 14 × 25 + 9 = 359, 14 × 40 + 13 = 573, and 14 × 71 + 1 = 995 also meet the conditions. If you write 188 chocolates as 12 boxes and 20 loose pieces, the total correct, but e wrong because 20 loose pieces fit fill one more box.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Why loose pieces number r must be less than 14? Write the reason with your own words.
z-m-08-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write one by one wetin you fit do with leftover pieces if r na 14, 15 and 20.

z-m-08-05.title: Length left after using 3.47m from a 10m ribbon 3.47 10
z-m-08-05.topic: Comparing methods for subtracting hundredths from whole number
z-m-08-05.goal: Compare ways to solve same problem, identify correct ones, estimate to remove wrong answers, and say which method suits these numbers with reason.
z-m-08-05.material:
A 3.47m piece was cut from 10m ribbon. Five friends find remaining length:
Mina: 10−3=7, then attach decimal part 0.47, so 7.47m.
Jiho: write 10 as 10.00, line up decimals, vertical subtraction gives 6.53m.
Haneul: change 3.47 to 3.5 and subtract, exactly 6.5m.
Raon: 10=1000/100 and 3.47=347/100, so difference 653/100=6.53m.
Soyeon: subtract 3 from 10 to make 7, then subtract 0.47, answer 6.53m. Mina answer is 7.47m. The answer 7.47m is her value. 10 3.47 3 10 7 0.47 7.47 10 10.00 6.53 3.47 3.5 6.5 10 1000 100 3.47 347 100 653 100 6.53 3 10 7 0.47 7 6.53
